name: Degerforsmålet
confidence_why: Åström 1888 says uncompounded Degerfors words carry the same stress as Standard Swedish and sets up the acute/grave/circumflex accent distinction, and Lindgren 1890 states the same system outright for the neighbouring Burträsk dialect (main stress on the first syllable, accent 1 on old monosyllables, accent 2 on old polysyllables), so the two descriptions agree on initial stress with a tonal accent and only a few adverbs, names and compounds carry final stress.

tone_statements.quote: I dialekten liksom i standardsvenskan finns åtskilliga exempel där kontrast mellan accent 1 och 2 föreligger. ... I materialet har 24 minimala par kunnat ställas upp i den kategorin. ... Förutom accent 1 och 2 förekommer cirkumflex accent i dialekten. ... i Rödåliden förekommer cirkumflex med apokope endast i ursprungligt långstaviga, tvåstaviga ord ... Ytterligare en avvikelse från standardsvenskan är att cirkumflex accent förekommer i dialekten och att det finns två huvudtyper, nämligen lång och kort cirkumflex. ... tone_statements.translation: In the dialect, as in standard Swedish, there are numerous examples where a contrast between accent 1 and 2 exists. ... In the material 24 minimal pairs could be set up in that category. ... Besides accent 1 and 2, circumflex accent occurs in the dialect. ... in Rödåliden circumflex with apocope occurs only in originally long-syllabled disyllabic words ... A further deviation from standard Swedish is that circumflex accent occurs in the dialect and that there are two main types, namely long and short circumflex. ... At the lexical level, however, the accent is always distinctive.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 5.1.2.1-5.1.2.2, pp. 55-56, and sec. 5.1.2.6, p. 62 (printed pagination)
tone_statements.summary: Accent 1 vs 2 (24 noun/verb minimal pairs) plus circumflex accent in apocopated originally long-syllable words (fryys 'frysa' vs frys 'fryser'); long/short circumflex differ mainly in quantity; circumflex cancelled in compounds. Auditory, 13 informants, perception tests, no F0. IPA marks lost.

sources.citation: Bruce, Gösta. 2004. An intonational typology of Swedish. In: Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2004, Nara, 175-178. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2004-41.
sources.quote: The phonological specification is whether a certain dialect type has a distinction between two word accents or not, while the phonetic issue concerns the more specific timing of the pitch accent gesture (in relation to the primary stress). For those dialects that have the word accent distinction the pitch gesture of accent I always has an earlier timing than that of accent II, thus an early vs. late differentiation. [...] A North Swedish type has been proposed earlier [13] [14]
sources.locator: p. 177, section 4.3 'Word accentuation' and section 5 with Table 1 ('North: word accent contrast yes, word accent timing very early')
sources.note: Table 1: the North type has the two-word-accent contrast (yes), 'very early' word-accent timing, a distinct focal accent realised as an extra (second) pitch peak, downslope tonal concatenation, post-focal downstep rather than deaccentuation, and compound secondary stress as pitch synchronisation point (yes/no); Far East (Finland) types lack the accent contrast. Typology explicitly built on Meyer 1937/1954 and Bruce & Gårding 1978.

sources.note: Two tonal word accents, accent I (HL*) and accent II (H*L), as elsewhere in Swedish; accent is the tonal layer of prominence on top of stress. In North Botnia dialects compounds without stress clash take final-element stress with accent I instead of initial accent II, analysed as a late-aligned floating L of the same HL gesture; a North Swedish phrase-level HL pattern with H two syllables before an accent-I stress is also described. No claim of a missing accent contrast (that is Överkalix only, see Källskog 1986).
